> "Loot X" is an ability that allows a figure to loot all loot tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles. If there are no loot tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range, the ability cannot be performed.

When a loot token is looted, it is removed from the map. If the looting figure is a monster, nothing else happens. If the looting figure is a character, they draw one card from the loot deck (unless the loot deck is empty).

**Key points:**
- If the loot card provides a random item, the character draws from the random item deck and can use it immediately.
- If the loot card provides money or resources, the character does not gain them until the end of the scenario.
- Characters must also loot any loot tokens or treasure tiles in their hex at the end of their turn (*End-of-Turn Looting*).
- Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.

(Rulebook)

# Advantage with Attack Modifier Cards in Frosthaven

With *advantage*, the attacker draws **two modifiers and uses one of them**. A monster always uses the better one, but a character may use either one.

## Rolling Modifiers

If the first draw is a *rolling modifier*, the attacker continues drawing additional modifiers one at a time until a non-rolling modifier is drawn, then draws one more modifier and ignores any rolling icon on it. 

The attacker then uses **all initial rolling modifiers and whichever of the last two modifiers they choose**.

If the first draw is not a rolling modifier but the second is, the rolling icon on the second modifier is still ignored.

## Resolving Ambiguity

When there is ambiguity about which modifier is better (e.g., comparing non-numeric effects like elemental infusions or negative conditions), **the attacker must use the one drawn first**. Any non-numeric effect is considered to have a positive but undefined value.

## Multiple Instances

An attack cannot gain multiple instances of advantage or disadvantage. If an attack has both advantage and disadvantage, it is considered to have neither.

Yes. According to the FAQ:

> Can I skip targets in a red hex AoE attack? Yes; a red hex AoE just determines the hexes where your potential targets are. Note - this is a change from the Gloomhaven 1e FAQ, and is to make it consistent with all other non-mandatory targeting.

In Gloomhaven (2nd Edition), **"Loot X"** is an ability that allows a figure to loot all money tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles. If there are no money tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range, the ability cannot be performed.

**How looting works:**

- **Money tokens:** When looted, the token is removed from the map. If a monster loots it, nothing else happens. If a character loots it, they place the token on their character mat.

- **Treasure tiles:** When looted, the tile is removed from the map. Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles. If the looted treasure tile is numbered, you reference that number in the Treasure Index and apply the effect. Only the looting character gains the reward (unless it's a random item design or random scenario). If a character gains a duplicate of an item they already own, they must give it to another character or sell it immediately.

*Source: Rulebook*

When a character performs a **long rest** in Gloomhaven (2nd Edition), they follow these three steps (Rulebook, passage 161):

# Advantage and Disadvantage with Attack Modifiers

**Basic mechanic:**
With *advantage*, the attacker draws two modifiers and uses one of them. A monster always uses the better one, but a character may use either one. With *disadvantage*, the attacker draws two modifiers and always uses the worse one.

**With rolling modifiers:**
If the first draw is a rolling modifier, the attacker draws additional modifiers one at a time until a non-rolling modifier is drawn, then draws one more modifier and ignores any rolling icon on it.

The first non-rolling modifier and the one after it are compared:
- **Advantage:** Use all initial rolling modifiers plus whichever of the last two modifiers you choose.
- **Disadvantage:** Ignore all initial rolling modifiers and use whichever of the last two modifiers is worse.

If the first draw is not rolling but the second is, the rolling icon on the second modifier is still ignored.

**Special cases:**
- An attack cannot have multiple instances of advantage or disadvantage. If it has both, it has neither.
- Any ranged attack on an adjacent enemy automatically gains *disadvantage*.
- When comparing non-numeric effects (like elemental infusions or conditions), the one drawn first is the worse one.

According to the FAQ:

> Only if it is not itself an ability, and it says something like "during your move ability." If an item allows you to perform another ability (like healing, damaging, destroying an obstacle, etc.), you need to finish your ability first.

The key rule from the Rulebook is:

> If an item provides an ability, it cannot be used during another ability.

**In short:** You can use an item mid-move or mid-attack **only if** the item text explicitly says "during your move" or "during your attack" (like Stun Powder saying "During your attack ability, add Stun to one attack"). If the item grants a separate ability—even a small one like healing or damage—you must finish your current move or attack first.
